title: Tenochtitlan
summary: México-Tenochtitlan, the Mexica island capital in Lake Texcoco, grew from a traditional founding in 1325 into the largest city in the Americas, until a Spanish and Indigenous allied siege destroyed it in 1521. Mexico City stands on its ruins.
card: Tenochtitlan was the Mexica city raised on an islet in Lake Texcoco, extended over the water and tied to the shore by causeways; from 1428 it led the Triple Alliance that ruled much of central Mexico. At its heart the twin-shrine Templo Mayor was rebuilt larger at least seven times between the fourteenth century and 1520. After the Toxcatl massacre, a smallpox epidemic and a siege of about 93 days, the city fell in August 1521 and the Spanish built their own capital over it.
what:
Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Mexica, a Nahua people whose migration traditions bring them from Aztlan, an island they placed somewhere to the north, into the Basin of Mexico; historians put those migrations roughly between 1150 and 1300. In the account Indigenous informants gave after the conquest, the god Huitzilopochtli told the Mexica to settle where they saw an eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus, and they found the sign on an islet in Lake Texcoco in the year 2 House (2 Casa), equated with 1325 CE. That date is a tradition, not an archaeological result: Eduardo Matos Moctezuma has said radiocarbon cannot resolve it, a 2019 planning panel weighed 1324, 1325 and 1364, and some researchers argue the founding story was reshaped after 1428 under the ruler Itzcóatl.

The city spread from the natural islet over land built out into the lake. Its sacred precinct, a paved plaza about 350 m on a side, held dozens of temples and ritual buildings; at the centre stood the Templo Mayor, a pyramid crowned by shrines to Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc. Excavations since 1978 have exposed at least seven complete enlargements, dated from Phase I (1325–1375) to Phase VII (1502–1520). Three causeways ran from the precinct toward Iztapalapa, Tlacopan and Tepeyac. In 1428 Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan allied after the defeat of Azcapotzalco, and Tenochtitlan became the leading partner of the empire that followed; in 1473 it absorbed Tlatelolco, its twin city immediately to the north.

Estimates of the population in 1519 run from about 75,000–95,000 to more than 200,000, depending on the assumed area (about 9.4 to 13.5 km²) and people per house. In May 1520 Spanish soldiers under Pedro de Alvarado killed Mexica nobles gathered for the Toxcatl festival; smallpox followed; and after a siege Bernal Díaz put at 93 days the city fell on 13 August 1521 (Julian; 23 August Gregorian). The Spanish razed it, began draining the lake, and built Mexico City on its ruins.

uncertainty.note: Start is the traditional founding year 2 House (2 Casa) = 1325 CE, drawn from post-conquest Indigenous testimony; a 2019 panel at the Museo del Templo Mayor weighed 1324, 1325 and 1364, and archaeology cannot fix the date (radiocarbon errors of up to about 50 years, per Matos Moctezuma). End is the fall of the city, 13 August 1521 Julian, converted to 23 August 1521 proleptic Gregorian (+10 days). The site has been continuously occupied since as Mexico City; that continuation belongs to a separate record.

how: Tenochtitlan's growth rested on water engineering, canoe transport and tribute. The Mexica extended a small natural islet into a city of built-up land and canals, and fed it partly from chinampas, cultivation beds raised in the shallow lake that UNESCO counts among the most productive farming systems known; the surviving remnant at Xochimilco is part of World Heritage property 412. Three causeways crossed the lake, but canoes did most of the hauling: López Luján estimates one man could move up to 1,200 kg by canoe against 23 kg carried on his back. The Templo Mayor was built from the basin's volcanic rocks (basalt, red tezontle, andesites), lake-bed soil and wood, with lime for plaster brought from the Tula region, and subject lakeside towns were obliged to supply and carry materials for each enlargement. After the 1428 war against Azcapotzalco, the conquests of the Triple Alliance channelled tribute to the capital, which outgrew its partners. The end came through a chain of shocks: the Toxcatl massacre of May 1520 turned an uneasy Spanish occupation into open war; the Spanish were driven out; smallpox, which Bernal Díaz traced to an African servant in Pánfilo de Narváez's company, spread through the region and killed the ruler Cuitláhuac; and Cortés's forces and their Indigenous allies blockaded and assaulted the island for about 93 days until Cuauhtémoc was captured on 13 August 1521 (Julian).
why_it_matters: Tenochtitlan was the largest city in the Americas of its day and the seat of the dominant power in central Mexico, so its fall decided the shape of the colonial order that followed. Because the Spanish chose to build the capital of New Spain on its ruins, the Mexica city still underlies Mexico City: UNESCO notes that the historic centre's street grid follows a colonial plan that was itself based on the structure of the Aztec capital, and one of the world's largest cities now covers the former island and most of the drained lake. The founding sign of the eagle on the cactus became Mexico's national coat of arms, and the 2025 commemorations of the city's 700th anniversary show that its origin story remains part of national identity. The conquest also opened a demographic catastrophe: the 1519–1520 smallpox epidemic is estimated to have killed 5–8 million people in Mexico, and later epidemics killed millions more. Had the city not been razed and its lake drained, the chinampa landscape that now survives only at Xochimilco might have survived far more widely. And without the chance discovery of the Coyolxauhqui monolith by electricity workers in 1978, the Templo Mayor's seven building phases might still lie buried, leaving the Mexica capital known mainly through conquerors' accounts and colonial-era Indigenous testimony.

perspectives.holder: Mexica tradition as recorded after the conquest; INAH's official commemoration (2025)
perspectives.account: The city was founded in the year 2 House (2 Casa), 1325 CE, where the Mexica saw the eagle on the cactus; INAH treats 26 July 1325 as the most accepted day and celebrated the 700th anniversary in July 2025.

perspectives.holder: Eduardo Matos Moctezuma and a 2019 planning panel at the Museo del Templo Mayor
perspectives.account: Founding a city was a process rather than a moment; radiocarbon cannot settle the year, 1324, 1325 and 1364 were all weighed, and a total solar eclipse of 13 April 1325 (Jesús Galindo's proposal) may have served as a mythic marker.

perspectives.holder: Ismael Arturo Montero García (Entre el cielo y el lago, 2025, as summarised by INAH)
perspectives.account: The founding story is a ritual consecration of the temple rather than a datable event, shaped into official history under Itzcóatl and Tlacaélel after the 1428 victory over Azcapotzalco; the mythic founding may have been set near the winter solstice.

perspectives.holder: Pedro de Alvarado and Spanish witnesses (Bernal Díaz; testimony of 1521 and 1529 reviewed by Olivier)
perspectives.account: Alvarado said he struck first because he had learned of a Mexica plan to free Motecuhzoma and kill the Spanish during the festival; Díaz accepted this and rejected Las Casas's charge that greed for the dancers' gold was the motive.

perspectives.holder: Nahua accounts (Sahagún's informants, Anales de Tlatelolco, Códice Aubin) and historians reading them
perspectives.account: The attack was a murderous slaughter of the Mexica nobility and celebrants gathered in the precinct during the festival; Kruell notes the Spanish sources say almost nothing about motive, while Olivier cautions against portraying the Mexica only as helpless victims.

perspectives.holder: Population in 1519: Jiménez Martínez (2022) versus Calnek (1970s–80s) and Smith (2005)
perspectives.account: Comparing densities with other cities and taking an area of 9.44 km², Jiménez Martínez estimates 75,000–95,000 people; Calnek argued for 150,000–200,000 (or 144,000 at 12 km² and 12,000 per km²), and Smith's tabulation gives 212,500 over 13.5 km².

audience_note: Describes a massacre during a religious festival (1520), a siege and the destruction of a city (1521), an epidemic with mass mortality, and human sacrifice in Mexica ritual. Some codex images show violence and disease.

importance.justification: Capital of the dominant Mesoamerican power at European contact, whose fall began colonial rule in mainland America and whose site is now one of the world's largest cities, so it should be visible from whole-planet view.

footprint.description: Island city of Tenochtitlan-Tlatelolco c. 1519 from Edward Calnek's (1986) large-scale reconstruction map, georeferenced against the 1935 Plano del Centro de la Ciudad de México and digitized by Andrew Sluyter (LandCover6k, 2016) to a 1,256 ha polygon, within 7% of the 1,350 ha in Smith (2005). This is a scholarly reconstruction map based on documentary and archaeological evidence, not a modern field survey; the excavated Templo Mayor zone (1.2 ha) is the only surveyed core.

phases.description: Phase I of the Templo Mayor; earliest temple in the published phase chronology.
Phase II, with partial extensions IIa–IIc of the main or northern façade.
Phase III enlargement on all four façades.
Phase IVa; limestone floor slabs from Puebla in two rooms beside the stairs.
Phase IVb; the Coyolxauhqui monolith placed at the foot of the stairs, found in 1978.
Phase VI, with a full renovation of the platform staircase (VIa).
Phase VII, the last pyramid, standing when the Spanish arrived in 1519.
The conquerors destroy the island city and begin draining the lake that surrounded it.
Remains buried beneath the colonial and later city, built on the ruins following the old city's structure.
Manuel Gamio identifies the Templo Mayor archaeologically in 1914; most of the structure stays buried.
After the chance find of the Coyolxauhqui monolith on 21 February 1978, the Proyecto Templo Mayor under Eduardo Matos Moctezuma exposes the pyramid's stages.
Excavated stages conserved in the 1.2 ha archaeological zone; seven field seasons to date, the later four directed by Leonardo López Luján.
